title: ECE Notes
text:
These notes accompany the Equivariant Covariance Estimator (ECE) project. The goal is to estimate and test for contemporaneous correlation between two time series in the presence of unknown mean shifts, without requiring explicit changepoint detection.
The notes combine theoretical derivations with R computations that verify the theory.

title: 2  Model Assumptions
text:
2.1 Error Structure
We observe input data sequences \(X = (X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) and \(Y = (Y_1, \ldots, Y_n)\). Each observation decomposes into a mean component and an error component:
\[
X_i = \theta_{x,i} + \varepsilon_{x,i}, \qquad Y_i = \theta_{y,i} + \varepsilon_{y,i}.
\]
The error terms \((\varepsilon_{x,i}, \varepsilon_{y,i})\) have zero mean and covariance matrix
\[
\Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_x^2 & \sigma_{xy} \\ \sigma_{xy} & \sigma_y^2 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
We assume there is no autocorrelation: for \(i \neq j\),
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_{x,i}, \varepsilon_{x,j})
= \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_{y,i}, \varepsilon_{y,j})
= \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_{x,i}, \varepsilon_{y,j})
= 0.
\]
Contemporaneous dependence between \(X\) and \(Y\) is captured by \(\sigma_{xy} = \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_{x,i}, \varepsilon_{y,i})\), the main quantity of interest in these notes.

title: 2  Model Assumptions
text:
2.2 Mean Structure
The mean components \(\theta_x = (\theta_{x,1}, \ldots, \theta_{x,n})\) and \(\theta_y = (\theta_{y,1}, \ldots, \theta_{y,n})\) are assumed to be piecewise constant. We call index \(i\) a change point when \(\theta_i \neq \theta_{i+1}\), and collect all change points in \(\tau = (\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_J)\) in ascending order. With \(\tau_0 = 0\) and \(\tau_{J+1} = n\), the shortest segment length is
\[
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \min_{0 \le j \le J} \{\tau_{j+1} - \tau_j\}, \qquad \Theta_L = \{\theta : \mathcal{L}(\theta) \ge L\}.
\]
This allows frequent mean shifts while ensuring a minimum spacing \(L\) between consecutive change points.

title: 3  Lagged Differences
text:
3.1 \(k\)-Lagged Estimator
Using circular indexing \(i := [(i-1) \bmod n] + 1\), define the \(k\)-lagged cross-product sum
\[
T_k(X, Y) = \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - X_{i+k})(Y_i - Y_{i+k}).
\]
We abbreviate \(T_k(X) := T_k(X,X)\) and similarly for \(Y\).

title: 3  Lagged Differences
text:
3.2 Circular Version
A practical issue with \(T_k\) is that the number of terms \(n - k\) shrinks as \(k\) grows, making comparisons across lags unequal. To fix this, we embed the index set on a circle by redefining
\[
i \;:=\; [(i - 1) \bmod n] + 1,
\]
so that index \(n+1\) wraps back to \(1\). Under this convention every lag uses exactly \(n\) differences. The circular \(k\)-lagged covariance estimator is
\[
\hat{\sigma}_k(X, Y) = \frac{1}{2n}\, T_k(X, Y).
\]
Like the non-circular version, \(\hat{\sigma}_k\) is unbiased for \(\sigma_{xy}\) whenever \(1 \le k < n\) and there are no mean shifts. It is slightly more efficient because it uses all \(n\) differences at every lag.

title: 3  Lagged Differences
text:
3.3 Bias Under Mean Shifts
When mean shifts are present the estimator is no longer unbiased. To see why, expand a single lagged difference:
\[
X_i - X_{i+k} = (\theta_{x,i} - \theta_{x,i+k}) + (\varepsilon_{x,i} - \varepsilon_{x,i+k}).
\]
Whenever \(i\) and \(i+k\) straddle a change point, the mean difference \(\theta_{x,i} - \theta_{x,i+k}\) is nonzero and contaminates the cross-product. The resulting bias in \(T_k\) is
\[
\mathbb{E}[T_k(X, Y)] = 2n\sigma_{xy} + k\,\omega_{xy},
\qquad \omega_{xy} = T_1(\theta_x, \theta_y),
\]
so the bias of \(\hat{\sigma}_k\) grows linearly in \(k\).

title: 3  Lagged Differences
text:
3.4 Equivariant Covariance Estimator (ECE)
Since \(\mathbb{E}[T_k(X,Y)/2n] = \sigma_{xy} + k\,\omega_{xy}/2n\), the quantity \(\sigma_{xy}\) is the intercept of a line in \(k\). Fitting this line at \(k=1,2\) and extracting the intercept gives the ECE:
\[
\hat{\sigma}_{xy} = \frac{1}{2n}\bigl(2T_1(X,Y) - T_2(X,Y)\bigr).
\]
By linearity of expectation, \(\mathbb{E}[\hat{\sigma}_{xy}] = \sigma_{xy}\), so ECE is unbiased under the piecewise-constant mean model.

title: 4  Bilinear Form
text:
4.1 Solving for \(A\)
Definition. An estimator \(\tilde{s}(X, Y) = X^T A Y\) for \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\) is called bilinear.
Expanding using \(X = \theta_x + \varepsilon_x\) and \(Y = \theta_y + \varepsilon_y\) and taking expectations gives
\[
\mathbb{E}[\tilde{s}(X, Y)] = \theta_x^T A \theta_y + \operatorname{tr}(A)\, \sigma_{xy}.
\]
For unbiasedness, \(A\) must satisfy
To reduce the search space, we impose a symmetry condition. Let \(C_k\) be the circulant shift matrix, which shifts a vector \(k\) positions to the right circularly.
Definition. A bilinear estimator is equivariant if \(\tilde{s}(C_k X, C_k Y) = \tilde{s}(X, Y)\) for all \(k\).
Lemma (Equivariant \(\Leftrightarrow\) Symmetric Circulant). Since \(\tilde{s}\) is a covariance estimator, \(A\) must be symmetric. The bilinear estimator \(X^T A Y\) is equivariant if and only if \(A\) is a symmetric circulant: \[
A = \operatorname{circ}(a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}, \ldots, a_1) = \begin{bmatrix}
a_0    & a_1    & \cdots & a_1    \\
a_1    & a_0    & \cdots & \vdots \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
a_1    & \cdots & a_1    & a_0
\end{bmatrix},
\] where \(a_k = a_{n-k}\) for all \(k\).
Proof. Since \(\tilde{s}(C_k X, C_k Y) = X^T(C_k^T A C_k)Y\), equivariance holds iff \(A = C_k^T A C_k\) for all \(k\), which is equivalent to \(A\) being circulant. Symmetry of \(A\) further requires \(a_k = a_{n-k}\), so \(A\) is a symmetric circulant. \(\square\)
This reduces the \(n^2\) free parameters of \(A\) to the \(n\) entries of its first row. Applying the unbiasedness constraints then uniquely determines \(A\), and the resulting estimator is exactly \(\hat{\sigma}_{xy}\).
Since \(A\) is a symmetric circulant, it is determined by \((a_0, \ldots, a_{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor})\). The unbiasedness conditions reduce to a linear system in these entries.
For a circulant \(A\), the condition \(\theta_x^T A \theta_y = 0\) for all piecewise-constant \(\theta_x, \theta_y \in \Theta_L\) is equivalent to requiring that the sum of all entries of every \(\ell \times \ell\) contiguous submatrix of \(A\) is zero, for \(\ell = L, \ldots, \lfloor n/2 \rfloor\). Denoting by \(A_\ell\) such a submatrix, this reads
\[
\|A_\ell\|_1 = 0, \qquad \ell = L, \ldots, \lfloor n/2 \rfloor.
\]
For a symmetric circulant, this sum depends only on \((a_0, \ldots, a_{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor})\) and takes the explicit form
\[
g(\ell) = \ell\, a_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{\min\{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor,\, \ell\}} 2(\ell - i)\, a_i + \sum_{i=\lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1}^{\ell} 2(\ell - i)\, a_{n-i}.
\]
For \(L = 2\), setting \(g(\ell) = 0\) for \(\ell = 2, 3\) and using \(a_0 = 1/n\) gives
\[
g(2) = 2a_0 + 2a_1 = 0 \implies a_1 = -a_0,
\] \[
g(3) = 3a_0 + 4a_1 + 2a_2 = 0 \implies a_2 = \tfrac{a_0}{2},
\]
and for \(\ell \geq 4\) one shows by induction that \(a_{\ell - 1} = 0\). Together with \(a_0 = 1/n\), this uniquely determines \(A\).

title: 4  Bilinear Form
text:
4.2 Matrix Form of ECE
Proposition. For \(L = 2\), the ECE \(\hat{\sigma}_{xy} = X^T A Y\) where \(A = \frac{1}{n}\operatorname{circ}(a)\) and
\[
a = \left(1,\; -1,\; \tfrac{1}{2},\; 0,\; \ldots,\; 0,\; \tfrac{1}{2},\; -1\right).
\]
Proof. Since \(T_k(X,Y) = ((I-C_k)X)^T((I-C_k)Y)\), we have \(T_k(X,Y) = X^T A_k Y\) where
\[
A_k = (I - C_k)^T(I - C_k) = 2I - C_k - C_k^T.
\]
Since \(C_k = \operatorname{circ}(e_k)\), we have \(A_k = \operatorname{circ}(\tilde{a}_k)\) where the first row \(\tilde{a}_k\) has \(+2\) at position \(0\), \(-1\) at position \(k\), \(-1\) at position \(n-k\), and \(0\) elsewhere.
Substituting into \(\hat{\sigma}_{xy} = \frac{1}{2n}(2T_1 - T_2)\),
\[
A = \frac{1}{2n}(2A_1 - A_2) = \frac{1}{2n}\bigl(2(2I - C_1 - C_1^T) - (2I - C_2 - C_2^T)\bigr) = \frac{1}{n}\operatorname{circ}(a). \quad\square
\]

title: 4  Bilinear Form
text:
4.3 Derivation of \(\mathbb{E}[X^T A Y]\)
Substituting \(X = \theta_x + \varepsilon_x\) and \(Y = \theta_y + \varepsilon_y\),
\[
X^T A Y = (\theta_x + \varepsilon_x)^T A (\theta_y + \varepsilon_y)
= \theta_x^T A \theta_y + \theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y + \varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y + \varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y.
\]
Taking expectations and using \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_x] = \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_y] = 0\),
\[
\mathbb{E}[X^T A Y] = \theta_x^T A \theta_y + \theta_x^T A \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_y] + \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_x]^T A \theta_y + \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y]
= \theta_x^T A \theta_y + \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y].
\]
For the remaining term, since \(\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y\) is a scalar,
\[
\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y = \operatorname{tr}(\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y).
\]
By the cyclic property of trace, \(\operatorname{tr}(\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y) = \operatorname{tr}(A \varepsilon_y \varepsilon_x^T)\). Taking the expectation and applying linearity,
\[
\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y] = \operatorname{tr}(A\, \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_y \varepsilon_x^T]) = \operatorname{tr}(A \cdot \sigma_{xy} I) = \sigma_{xy}\operatorname{tr}(A),
\]
where we used \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_y \varepsilon_x^T] = \sigma_{xy} I\).
Therefore,
\[
\mathbb{E}[X^T A Y] = \theta_x^T A \theta_y + \sigma_{xy}\operatorname{tr}(A). \qquad \square
\]

title: 4  Bilinear Form
text:
4.4 Derivation of \(\operatorname{Var}(X^T A Y)\)
Using the same decomposition, write \(X^T A Y = \theta_x^T A \theta_y + \theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y + \varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y + \varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y\). Since the first term is a constant, it does not contribute to the variance, so
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X^T A Y) = \operatorname{Var}(\theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y + \varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y + \varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y).
\]
Expanding,
\[\begin{align*}
\operatorname{Var}(X^T A Y) &= \operatorname{Var}(\theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y) + \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y) + \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y) \\
&\quad + 2\operatorname{Cov}(\theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y,\, \varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y) \\
&\quad + 2\operatorname{Cov}(\theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y,\, \varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y) \\
&\quad + 2\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y,\, \varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y).
\end{align*}\]






Derivation of each term





Term 1: \(\operatorname{Var}(\theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y)\). Since \(\theta_x^T A\) is a fixed row vector, this is the variance of a linear form in \(\varepsilon_y\):
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y) = \theta_x^T A \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_y) A^T \theta_x = \sigma_y^2\, \theta_x^T A A^T \theta_x = \sigma_y^2\, \theta_x^T A^2 \theta_x,
\]
where the last equality uses symmetry of \(A\).
Term 2: \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y)\). By the same argument, \(A \theta_y\) is a fixed vector, so
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y) = \theta_y^T A^T \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_x) A \theta_y = \sigma_x^2\, \theta_y^T A^2 \theta_y.
\]
Term 3: \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y)\). Apply the eigendecomposition \(A = Q\Lambda Q^T\) and let \(z_x = Q^T \varepsilon_x / \sigma_x\), \(z_y = Q^T \varepsilon_y / \sigma_y\), so that \(z_x, z_y \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\) with \(\operatorname{Cov}(z_x, z_y) = \rho I\) where \(\rho = \sigma_{xy}/(\sigma_x \sigma_y)\). Applying the eigendecomposition,
\[
\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y = \sigma_x \sigma_y\, z_x^T \Lambda z_y = \sigma_x \sigma_y \sum_i \lambda_i z_{x,i} z_{y,i}.
\]
Since \(\operatorname{Cov}(z_x, z_y) = \rho I\) is diagonal, the pairs \((z_{x,i}, z_{y,i})\) are independent across \(i\), so
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y) = \sigma_x^2 \sigma_y^2 \sum_i \lambda_i^2\, \operatorname{Var}(z_{x,i} z_{y,i}).
\]
For each \(i\), \((z_{x,i}, z_{y,i})\) is a standard bivariate Gaussian with correlation \(\rho\), so \(\operatorname{Var}(z_{x,i} z_{y,i}) = 1 + \rho^2\) (see Appendix). Therefore,
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y) = \sigma_x^2 \sigma_y^2 (1 + \rho^2)\operatorname{tr}(A^2) = (\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + \sigma_{xy}^2)\operatorname{tr}(A^2).
\]
Term 4: \(\operatorname{Cov}(\theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y,\, \varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y)\). Since \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_x] = \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_y] = 0\), both terms have zero expectation, so the covariance reduces to
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(\theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y,\, \varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y) = \mathbb{E}[(\theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y)(\varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y)] = \theta_x^T A\, \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_y \varepsilon_x^T]\, A^T \theta_y = \sigma_{xy}\, \theta_x^T A^2 \theta_y,
\]
where we used \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_y \varepsilon_x^T] = \sigma_{xy} I\) and symmetry of \(A\).
Terms 5 and 6: \(\operatorname{Cov}(\theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y,\, \varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y)\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y,\, \varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y)\). Since all terms have zero expectation, both covariances reduce to expectations of products involving one linear and one bilinear form in \((\varepsilon_x, \varepsilon_y)\). These are third-order moments of the zero-mean jointly Gaussian vector \((\varepsilon_x, \varepsilon_y)\), and all odd-order moments of a zero-mean Gaussian vanish. Therefore,
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(\theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y,\, \varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y) = 0, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y,\, \varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y) = 0.
\]



Collecting all terms,
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X^T A Y) = \sigma_y^2\, \theta_x^T A^2 \theta_x + \sigma_x^2\, \theta_y^T A^2 \theta_y + 2\sigma_{xy}\, \theta_x^T A^2 \theta_y + (\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + \sigma_{xy}^2)\operatorname{tr}(A^2).
\]
The noise contribution \((\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + \sigma_{xy}^2)\operatorname{tr}(A^2) = O(1/n)\) by the lower bound on \(\operatorname{tr}(A^2)\) (see Appendix B), which shows the estimator is consistent.

title: 4  Bilinear Form
text:
4.5 Solving for \(A\) (\(L > 2\))
For \(L > 2\), the unbiasedness constraints leave a multi-dimensional solution space for \(a\), so we have freedom to optimize. The full variance is
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X^T A Y) = \sigma_y^2\, \theta_x^T A^2 \theta_x + \sigma_x^2\, \theta_y^T A^2 \theta_y + 2\sigma_{xy}\, \theta_x^T A^2 \theta_y + (\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + \sigma_{xy}^2)\operatorname{tr}(A^2).
\]
Since \(\theta_x\) and \(\theta_y\) are unknown, the signal-dependent terms cannot be minimized directly. The only term we can control is the noise term \((\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + \sigma_{xy}^2)\operatorname{tr}(A^2)\), which for fixed noise levels reduces to minimizing \(\operatorname{tr}(A^2)\). This gives the optimization problem
\[
\min_{a \in \mathbb{R}^n} \operatorname{tr}(A^2) \quad \text{subject to} \quad \|A_\ell\|_1 = 0,\ \ell = L, \ldots, \lfloor n/2 \rfloor, n, \quad \operatorname{tr}(A) = 1,
\]
where \(A = \operatorname{circ}(a)\).
Reducing to a norm minimization. Since \(A = \operatorname{circ}(a)\) is a circulant, every row of \(A\) is a cyclic permutation of \(a\) and therefore has the same squared norm \(\|a\|^2\). The Frobenius norm of \(A\) is thus
\[
\|A\|_F^2 = n\|a\|^2.
\]
Since \(A\) is symmetric, \(\operatorname{tr}(A^2) = \operatorname{tr}(A^T A) = \|A\|_F^2 = n\|a\|^2\). Minimizing \(\operatorname{tr}(A^2)\) is therefore equivalent to minimizing \(\|a\|^2\). Because the unbiasedness constraints are linear in \(a\), the problem reduces to
\[
\min_{a \in \mathbb{R}^n} \|a\|^2 \quad \text{subject to} \quad \|A_\ell\|_1 = 0,\ \ell = L, \ldots, \lfloor n/2 \rfloor, n, \quad \operatorname{tr}(A) = 1,
\]
where \(A = \operatorname{circ}(a)\). Both sets of constraints are linear in \(a\), so this is a quadratic program with a unique solution — the minimum-norm point in the feasible affine subspace.

title: 4  Bilinear Form
text:
4.6 Regression Approach
A natural way to estimate \(\sigma_{xy}\) is to exploit the linear relationship \(\mathbb{E}[T_k(X,Y)] = 2n\sigma_{xy} + k\,\omega_{xy}\) (established in the Lagged Differences chapter). Stacking \(k = 1, \ldots, L\) gives a linear model
\[
\mathbb{E}[R] = K\beta,
\qquad
K = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ 1 & L \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times 2},
\quad
\beta = \begin{pmatrix} 2n\sigma_{xy} \\ \omega_{xy} \end{pmatrix},
\]
where \(R_k = T_k(X,Y)\). The OLS estimate is \(\hat\beta = (K^TK)^{-1}K^T R\), and the regression estimator of \(\sigma_{xy}\) is its first component rescaled:
\[
\tilde\sigma_{xy} = \frac{1}{2n}\, e_1^T(K^TK)^{-1}K^T R = \sum_{k=1}^L c_k R_k,
\]
where \(c_k = \frac{1}{2n}\bigl[(K^TK)^{-1}K^T\bigr]_{1k}\) are the coefficients from the first row of \(\frac{1}{2n}(K^TK)^{-1}K^T\).
Relationship \(T_k(X,Y) = X^T A_k Y\). Since
\[
T_k(X,Y) = \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - X_{i+k})(Y_i - Y_{i+k}) = \bigl((I - C_k)X\bigr)^T\bigl((I - C_k)Y\bigr),
\]
we have \(T_k(X,Y) = X^T A_k Y\) with
\[
A_k = (I - C_k)^T(I - C_k) = 2I - C_k - C_k^T.
\]
Substituting \(R_k = X^T A_k Y\) into the regression estimator,
\[
\tilde\sigma_{xy} = \sum_{k=1}^L c_k R_k = X^T A Y,
\]
so the regression estimator is a bilinear form \(X^T A Y\) with
\[
A = \sum_{k=1}^L c_k\, A_k.
\]
Since each \(A_k = 2I - C_k - C_k^T\) is a symmetric circulant, \(A\) is also a symmetric circulant, determined by its first row \(\tilde{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n\).
First row of the regression matrix. Writing \(A_k = \operatorname{circ}(a_k)\) where \(a_k\) denotes the first row of \(A_k\), linearity of the circulant map gives
\[
A = \operatorname{circ}(\tilde{a}), \qquad \tilde{a} = \sum_{k=1}^L c_k\, a_k.
\]
From \(A_k = 2I - C_k - C_k^T\) and the circulant form of \(C_k\) (see Mathematical Background), the first row is \(a_k = 2e_0 - e_k - e_{n-k}\), where \(e_j\) denotes the \(j\)-th standard basis vector.

title: 4  Bilinear Form
text:
4.7 Feasibility of the Regression Estimator
To show that \(\tilde{a}\) is the minimum-norm solution, we must verify it is feasible, i.e., that it satisfies the trace and unbiasedness constraints.
The regression estimator is the bilinear form \(X^T A Y\) with \(A = \sum_{k=1}^L c_k A_k\), where \(c_k = H_{1,k} = \frac{2L+1-3k}{nL(L-1)}\). Since we evaluate \(g(\ell)\) only for \(\ell \geq L\), every \(k \leq L\) satisfies \(k \leq \ell\), so the Lemma (see Other Mathematical Results) gives \(\mathbf{1}_\ell^T A_k \mathbf{1}_\ell = 2k\). By linearity, \[g(\ell) = \mathbf{1}_\ell^T A\, \mathbf{1}_\ell = 2\sum_{k=1}^L c_k k,\] which is independent of \(\ell\). Both constraints then reduce to evaluating \(\sum_k c_k\) and \(\sum_k c_k k\) via the closed form of \(c_k\).
Trace constraint: \(\operatorname{tr}(A) = 1\). Since \(\operatorname{tr}(A_k) = \operatorname{tr}(2I - C_k - C_k^T) = 2n\) (as \(C_k\) has no fixed points for \(k \geq 1\)), we have \(\operatorname{tr}(A) = 2n\sum_k c_k\). Applying the Gaussian sum \(\sum_{k=1}^L k = \frac{L(L+1)}{2}\), \[\sum_{k=1}^L c_k = \frac{1}{nL(L-1)}\left[(2L+1)L - \frac{3L(L+1)}{2}\right] = \frac{1}{n(L-1)}\cdot\frac{L-1}{2} = \frac{1}{2n}.\] Therefore \(\operatorname{tr}(A) = 2n \cdot \frac{1}{2n} = 1\). \(\square\)
Unbiasedness: \(g(\ell) = 0\) for \(\ell = L, \ldots, \lfloor n/2 \rfloor\). For \(\ell \geq L\), \(g(\ell) = 2\sum_k c_k k\). Applying the Gaussian sums \(\sum_{k=1}^L k = \frac{L(L+1)}{2}\) and \(\sum_{k=1}^L k^2 = \frac{L(L+1)(2L+1)}{6}\), \[\sum_{k=1}^L c_k k = \frac{1}{nL(L-1)}\left[(2L+1)\frac{L(L+1)}{2} - \frac{3L(L+1)(2L+1)}{6}\right] = \frac{(2L+1)L(L+1)}{nL(L-1)}\left[\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2}\right] = 0.\] Therefore \(g(\ell) = 0\) for all \(\ell \geq L\). \(\square\)

title: 4  Bilinear Form
section: 4.8 The Regression Estimator is the Minimum-Norm Estimator
text:
4.8 The Regression Estimator is the Minimum-Norm Estimator
Having established feasibility, it remains to show that \(\tilde{a}\) is the minimum-norm feasible solution.
Setup. Since the unbiasedness constraints are homogeneous (\(Ga = 0\)), every feasible \(a\) lies in \(\mathrm{null}(G)\). The trace constraint \(\mathrm{tr}(A) = 1\) is the only inhomogeneous condition, cutting out an affine hyperplane within \(\mathrm{null}(G)\): \[F = \{a \in \mathrm{null}(G) : \mathrm{tr}(A) = 1\}.\] Let \(a^* \in F\) be the minimum-norm feasible solution. We will show \(a^* = \tilde{a}\) by writing \(a^* = \tilde{a} + w\) with \(w = a^* - \tilde{a}\) and expanding: \[\|a^*\|^2 = \|\tilde{a}\|^2 + \|w\|^2 + 2\langle\tilde{a}, w\rangle.\] Steps 1 and 2 below show \(\langle\tilde{a}, w\rangle = 0\), so the expansion reduces to \[\|a^*\|^2 = \|\tilde{a}\|^2 + \|w\|^2.\] Since \(a^*\) is optimal and \(\tilde{a}\) is feasible, \(\|a^*\|^2 \leq \|\tilde{a}\|^2\), so \[\|a^*\|^2 = \|\tilde{a}\|^2 + \|w\|^2 \leq \|\tilde{a}\|^2 \implies \|w\|^2 \leq 0.\] Therefore \(w = 0\) and \(a^* = \tilde{a}\).
Step 1: Characterize vectors satisfying \((*)\).
Since both \(a^*, \tilde{a} \in F\), the difference \(w = a^* - \tilde{a}\) satisfies \(Gw = 0\) (as both \(Ga^* = 0\) and \(G\tilde{a} = 0\)) and \(\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{circ}(w)) = \mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{circ}(a^*)) - \mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{circ}(\tilde{a})) = 1 - 1 = 0\). Since \(\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{circ}(w)) = nw_0\), we have \(w_0 = 0\). So \(w\) satisfies \[Gw = 0, \quad w_0 = 0. \tag{$*$}\]
Let \(w\) satisfy \((*)\). The constraint matrix \(G\) has entries \(G_{\ell,0} = \ell\) and \(G_{\ell,k} = 2(\ell-k)^+\) for \(k \geq 1\), so \(Gw = 0\) requires for each \(\ell = L, \ldots, \lfloor n/2 \rfloor\):
\[\ell\, w_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor} 2(\ell - k)^+\, w_k = 0.\]
We analyze this system by applying a first-difference operator twice. For any matrix \(B\) with \(r\) rows, define \(M(B)\) as the \((r-1) \times r\) bidiagonal matrix applied to \(B\):
\[M(B) = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} B,\]
so that \(M(B)_\ell = B_{\ell+1} - B_\ell\). We write \(M^2G\) as shorthand for \(M(M(G))\) — applying the operator twice sequentially, each time with a smaller matrix of appropriate dimensions. Since \(Gw = 0\) implies \(M(G)w = 0\) and \(M(M(G))w = 0\), each application yields simpler conditions.
Step 1a: Show \(w_k = 0\) for \(k > L\).
First application (\(M(G)w = 0\)). Subtracting the \(\ell\)-th row from the \((\ell+1)\)-th gives
\[w_0 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{\ell} w_k = 0, \qquad \ell = L, \ldots, \lfloor n/2 \rfloor - 1.\]
The resulting matrix \(MG\) has a column of \(1\)s in position \(k=0\) and \(2\)s in positions \(k = 1, \ldots, \ell\) (filling in one more entry per row):
\[MG = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & \cdots & 2 & 0 & 0 & \cdots \\ 1 & 2 & \cdots & 2 & 2 & 0 & \cdots \\ 1 & 2 & \cdots & 2 & 2 & 2 & \cdots \\ \vdots & & & & & & \ddots \end{pmatrix}.\]
Second application (\(M(M(G))w = 0\)). Subtracting consecutive equations from \(M(G)w = 0\) gives \(2w_{\ell+1} = 0\) for each \(\ell = L, \ldots, \lfloor n/2 \rfloor - 2\), so \(w_k = 0\) for all \(k > L\).
The matrix \(M(M(G))\) has exactly one nonzero entry per row — a \(2\) in column \(\ell + 1\) — making the zero conditions on each \(w_k\) explicit:
\[M(M(G)) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \cdots & 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 & \cdots \\ 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & 2 & 0 & \cdots \\ 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 & \cdots \\ \vdots & & & & & & \ddots \end{pmatrix}.\]
Step 1b: Characterize \((w_1, \ldots, w_L)\).
Having zeroed out \(w_k\) for \(k > L\), we need two conditions on the remaining entries \((w_1, \ldots, w_L)\). We obtain these by working back through \(MGw = 0\) and \(Gw = 0\) at \(\ell = L\) — each provides one independent condition, and no further applications of \(M\) are needed to characterize the null space.
Recall from Step 1a that \(M(G)w = 0\) gives \[w_0 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{\ell} w_k = 0, \qquad \ell = L, \ldots, \lfloor n/2 \rfloor - 1.\] Setting \(\ell = L\) and substituting \(w_k = 0\) for \(k > L\) gives \(w_0 + 2\sum_{k=1}^L w_k = 0\). Since \(w_0 = 0\) by \((*)\), this forces \(\sum_{k=1}^L w_k = 0\).
Similarly, recall from Step 1a that \(Gw = 0\) gives \(\ell\, w_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor} 2(\ell-k)^+\, w_k = 0\). Setting \(\ell = L\) and splitting the sum: \[L\, w_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{L} 2(L-k)^+\, w_k + \sum_{k=L+1}^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor} 2(L-k)^+\, w_k = 0.\] The second sum vanishes since \((L-k)^+ = 0\) for \(k > L\), and \(w_0 = 0\) by \((*)\), leaving \(\sum_{k=1}^L 2(L-k)\, w_k = 0\). Expanding and applying \(\sum_{k=1}^L w_k = 0\) gives \(\sum_{k=1}^L k\, w_k = 0\).
Therefore the vectors satisfying \((*)\) are exactly those with \(w_0 = 0\), \(w_k = 0\) for \(k > L\), and \((w_1, \ldots, w_L)\) satisfying
\[\sum_{k=1}^L w_k = 0, \qquad \sum_{k=1}^L k\,w_k = 0.\]
To summarize, each level of differentiation contributes one layer of structure:



Equation
Conclusion




\(M(M(G))w = 0\)
\(w_k = 0\) for \(k > L\)


\(M(G)w = 0\) at \(\ell = L\)
\(\sum_{k=1}^L w_k = 0\)


\(Gw = 0\) at \(\ell = L\)
\(\sum_{k=1}^L k\, w_k = 0\)



Step 2: Show \(\tilde{a} \perp w\).
Since \(\tilde{a} = \sum_{k=1}^L c_k \tilde{a}_k\), by linearity of the inner product: \[\langle \tilde{a}, w \rangle = \sum_{k=1}^L c_k \langle \tilde{a}_k, w \rangle.\]
Since \(\tilde{a}_k = 2e_0 - e_k - e_{n-k}\), \[\langle \tilde{a}_k, w \rangle = 2w_0 - w_k - w_{n-k}.\]
From Step 1: \(w_0 = 0\), and for \(k \in \{1, \ldots, L\}\) we have \(n - k > L\), so \(w_{n-k} = 0\). Therefore \(\langle \tilde{a}_k, w \rangle = -w_k\), and \[\langle \tilde{a}, w \rangle = -\sum_{k=1}^L c_k\, w_k.\]
Since \(c_k = \frac{2L+1-3k}{nL(L-1)}\) is affine in \(k\),
\[\sum_{k=1}^L c_k\, w_k = \frac{2L+1}{nL(L-1)} \sum_{k=1}^L w_k - \frac{3}{nL(L-1)} \sum_{k=1}^L k\,w_k = 0,\]
where both sums vanish by Step 1. Therefore \(\langle \tilde{a}, w \rangle = 0\) for all \(w\) satisfying \((*)\). \(\square\)

title: 5  Z-Test
text:
5.1 Diagnostics
Define the lag-\(k\) cross-product statistic \(T_k(X, Y) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (X_i - X_{i+k})(Y_i - Y_{i+k})\), and let \[
Z = \begin{pmatrix} Z_1 \\ Z_2 \\ Z_3 \\ Z_4 \\ Z_5 \\ Z_6 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} T_1(X,X) \\ T_2(X,X) \\ T_1(Y,Y) \\ T_2(Y,Y) \\ T_1(X,Y) \\ T_2(X,Y) \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The proof applies the Multivariate Delta Method in three steps:
Step 1. Show that \[
\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}(Z - \mu_Z) \xrightarrow{d} N(\mathbf{0}, \Sigma_Z), \quad \mu_Z = \mathbb{E}[Z].
\]
Step 2. Compute \(\Sigma_Z = \mathrm{Cov}(Z)\).
Step 3. Define \[
g(Z) = \frac{2Z_5 - Z_6}{\sqrt{(2Z_1 - Z_2)(2Z_3 - Z_4)}} = \hat\rho.
\] Since \(g(\mu_Z) = \rho\), the multivariate delta method gives \[
\sqrt{n}(\hat\rho - \rho) \xrightarrow{d} N(0,\, v^2), \quad v^2 = \nabla g(\mu_Z)^\top \Sigma_Z\, \nabla g(\mu_Z).
\]
To verify the formulas, we simulate scenario 2 (\(n = 1000\), \(L = 4\), \(r = 0.3\)) under two error distributions and compare the empirical covariance matrix of \(Z\) to the theoretical \(\Sigma_Z\).
For each error type, we run 500 outer replicates. In each replicate, we draw 10 independent datasets, compute \(Z\) for each, and take their sample covariance as one estimate of \(\Sigma_Z\). Each panel in the grid below shows the distribution of residuals (estimated minus theoretical) for one entry of \(\Sigma_Z\) across the 500 replicates. The red line marks zero (no bias) and the orange line marks the sample mean. The p-value is from a one-sample t-test of whether the mean residual is zero.

title: 5  Z-Test
text:
Test: \(Var(\hat{\rho})\) is Scale-Invariant





We can define the asymptotic variance of \(\hat{\rho}\) as \[
v^2 = \frac{1}{n}\left[
(1-\rho^2)\!\left(\frac{\omega_x^2}{\sigma_x^2} + \frac{\omega_y^2}{\sigma_y^2} - \frac{2\rho\,\omega_{xy}}{\sigma_x\sigma_y}\right)
+ \frac{\rho^2}{4}(\kappa_{40} + 2\kappa_{22} + \kappa_{04})
- \rho(\kappa_{31} + \kappa_{13})
+ \kappa_{22} + \frac{5}{2}(1-\rho^2)^2
\right].
\]
Since \(\widehat\rho(aX, bY) = \widehat\rho(X, Y)\) for any \(a, b > 0\), the asymptotic variance \(v^2\) must be invariant under \(X \to aX\), \(Y \to bY\). We verify this term by term.
\(\omega\) terms. Scaling \(X\) by \(a\) sends \(\theta_x \to a\theta_x\), so \(\omega_x^2 \to a^2\omega_x^2\) and \(\sigma_x \to a\sigma_x\). Similarly \(\omega_y \to b\omega_y\), \(\omega_{xy} \to ab\,\omega_{xy}\). The ratios \[
\frac{\omega_x^2}{\sigma_x^2} \to \frac{a^2\omega_x^2}{a^2\sigma_x^2} = \frac{\omega_x^2}{\sigma_x^2}, \qquad
\frac{\rho\,\omega_{xy}}{\sigma_x\sigma_y} \to \frac{\rho\cdot ab\,\omega_{xy}}{a\sigma_x\cdot b\sigma_y} = \frac{\rho\,\omega_{xy}}{\sigma_x\sigma_y}
\] are unchanged.
\(\kappa\) terms. The \(\kappa_{rs}\) are cumulants of the standardized errors \(\varepsilon_x/\sigma_x\) and \(\varepsilon_y/\sigma_y\). Scaling \(X\) by \(a\) scales both \(\varepsilon_x\) and \(\sigma_x\) by \(a\), leaving the ratio unchanged, so all \(\kappa_{rs}\) are invariant. \(\rho\) is invariant by definition.
Therefore \(v^2\) is scale-invariant, and we may study \(X/\sigma_x\), \(Y/\sigma_y\) in place of \(X\), \(Y\) without loss of generality. Setting \(\sigma_x = \sigma_y = 1\):
\[
v^2 = \frac{1}{n}\left[
(1-\rho^2)\!\left(\omega_x^2 + \omega_y^2 - 2\rho\,\omega_{xy}\right)
+ \frac{\rho^2}{4}(\kappa_{40} + 2\kappa_{22} + \kappa_{04})
- \rho(\kappa_{31} + \kappa_{13})
+ \kappa_{22} + \frac{5}{2}(1-\rho^2)^2
\right].
\]

title: 6  Multiplier Bootstrap Test
text:
6.1 Notation
We test the hypotheses \[H_0: \Sigma = I_p \quad \text{vs} \quad H_1: \Sigma \neq I_p.\] Equivalently, this is a test of whether all off-diagonal entries \(\sigma_{xy} = 0\), which are precisely the quantities estimated by the ECE.
Outline. The Multiplier Bootstrap provides a distribution-free null distribution for a sum of mean-zero independent terms. The ECE satisfies neither condition directly: its summands are neither mean-zero nor independent. We address each in turn. First, we reparametrize the ECE as a sum of terms \(s_i^{(k)}\) that are mean-zero under \(H_0\). Second, we partition these terms into three subsequences, each comprising independent terms. Each subsequence yields a p-value via the Multiplier Bootstrap. Finally, since the three subsequences are mutually dependent, we combine their p-values using the Cauchy Combination Test.
Using circular indexing \(i := [(i-1) \bmod n] + 1\), define the \(k\)-lagged sum \[T_k(X, Y) = \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - X_{i+k})(Y_i - Y_{i+k}).\]
For notational convenience, define \(s_i^{(k)} = (X_i - X_{i+k})(Y_i - Y_{i+k})\), so that \[T_k(X,Y) = \sum_{i=1}^n s_i^{(k)}.\]

title: 6  Multiplier Bootstrap Test
text:
6.2 Multiplier Bootstrap
The Multiplier Bootstrap requires each summand to be mean-zero. The terms \(s_i^{(k)}\) do not satisfy this directly.
Making Terms Mean Zero.
Under circular indexing, shifting all indices by 1 leaves \(T_1\) unchanged: \[T_1(X,Y) = \sum_{i=1}^n s_i^{(1)} = \sum_{i=1}^n s_{i+1}^{(1)}.\] Therefore \(2T_1(X,Y) = \sum_{i=1}^n \left(s_i^{(1)} + s_{i+1}^{(1)}\right)\), and the ECE numerator becomes \[2T_1(X,Y) - T_2(X,Y) = \sum_{i=1}^n \underbrace{\left(s_i^{(1)} + s_{i+1}^{(1)} - s_i^{(2)}\right)}_{S_i}.\]






Proof: \(S_i\) is mean-zero under \(H_0\)





Define \(h_i^{(k)} = (\theta_{x,i} - \theta_{x,i+k})(\theta_{y,i} - \theta_{y,i+k})\) and \(e_i^{(k)} = (\varepsilon_{x,i} - \varepsilon_{x,i+k})(\varepsilon_{y,i} - \varepsilon_{y,i+k})\). Since cross terms have mean zero, \(\mathbb{E}[s_i^{(k)}] = h_i^{(k)} + 2\sigma_{xy}\). Therefore \[\mathbb{E}[S_i] = h_i^{(1)} + h_{i+1}^{(1)} - h_i^{(2)} + 2\sigma_{xy}.\] Under \(H_0\) (\(\sigma_{xy} = 0\)), it remains to show \(h_i^{(1)} + h_{i+1}^{(1)} - h_i^{(2)} = 0\). We consider two cases.
If there is a change point at \(i\): minimum segment length 2 forces \(\theta_{i+1} = \theta_{i+2}\), so \(h_{i+1}^{(1)} = 0\) and \(h_i^{(2)} = h_i^{(1)}\). Hence \(h_i^{(1)} + 0 - h_i^{(1)} = 0\).
If there is a change point at \(i+1\): then \(\theta_i = \theta_{i+1}\), so \(h_i^{(1)} = 0\) and \(h_i^{(2)} = h_{i+1}^{(1)}\). Hence \(0 + h_{i+1}^{(1)} - h_{i+1}^{(1)} = 0\).
If there is no change point at either index, all terms are zero. Hence \(\mathbb{E}[S_i] = 0\) under \(H_0\).









Code: \(S_i\) is mean-zero under \(H_0\)

Making Terms Independent.
Each \(S_i\) depends only on observations \(X_i, X_{i+1}, X_{i+2}\) (and the same for \(Y\)), so \(S_i\) and \(S_j\) are independent whenever \(|i - j| \geq 3\). This motivates partitioning by residue mod 3: \[\{S_1, S_4, S_7, \ldots\}, \quad \{S_2, S_5, S_8, \ldots\}, \quad \{S_3, S_6, S_9, \ldots\}.\] Within each subsequence, consecutive terms are at least 3 apart, so the terms are independent. However, the three subsequences share observations and are mutually dependent, so their p-values cannot be combined trivially.

title: 6  Multiplier Bootstrap Test
text:
6.3 Cauchy Combination Test
Given p-values \(p_1, p_2, p_3\) from the three subsequences, the CCT statistic is \[T = \sum_{j=1}^3 w_j \tan\!\left(\left(\tfrac{1}{2} - p_j\right)\pi\right),\] where \(w_j > 0\) are weights with \(\sum_j w_j = 1\), typically \(w_j = 1/3\). Under \(H_0\), each \(p_j\) is uniformly distributed on \([0,1]\), so each summand is standard Cauchy. The key property of the CCT is that \(T\) is approximately standard Cauchy under \(H_0\) regardless of the dependence structure among the \(p_j\). The combined p-value is the upper-tail probability \(p = 1 - F_{\mathrm{Cauchy}}(T)\), where \(F_{\mathrm{Cauchy}}(t) = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{\arctan(t)}{\pi}\) is the standard Cauchy CDF. Substituting, \[p = 1 - \frac{1}{2} - \frac{\arctan(T)}{\pi} = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{\arctan(T)}{\pi}.\]






Code: Combined P-value is Uniform Under \(H_0\)

title: 7  Parametric Bootstrap Test
text:
7.1 Parametric Bootstrap Test
Let \(S_i \in \mathbb{R}^p\) denote the vector of lag terms across all pairs at index \(i\). To test \(H_0\), we need the variance of \(\bar{S} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n S_i\).
Since \(S_i\) depends only on observations at indices \(i, i+1, i+2\), terms separated by 3 or more indices are independent. The variance therefore has bandwidth 2: \[\begin{align*}
\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\bar{S}\right) &= \frac{1}{n^2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n \operatorname{Var}(S_i) + \sum_{i=1}^n\bigl[\operatorname{Cov}(S_i, S_{i+1}) + \operatorname{Cov}(S_{i+1}, S_i)\bigr]\right. \\
&\quad\left. + \sum_{i=1}^n\bigl[\operatorname{Cov}(S_i, S_{i+2}) + \operatorname{Cov}(S_{i+2}, S_i)\bigr]\right).
\end{align*}\] Plugging in \(\operatorname{Var}(S_i) = \mathbb{E}[S_i S_i^\top]\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(S_i, S_{i+k}) = \mathbb{E}[S_i S_{i+k}^\top]\) and estimating by sample quantities gives \[V := \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}\!\left(\bar{S}\right) = \frac{1}{n^2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n S_i S_i^\top + \sum_{i=1}^{n}\!\left(S_i S_{i+1}^\top + S_{i+1} S_i^\top\right) + \sum_{i=1}^{n}\!\left(S_i S_{i+2}^\top + S_{i+2} S_i^\top\right)\right).\]
Parametric Bootstrap Test. Under \(H_0\), \(\bar{S} \approx N(0, V)\) by the CLT. This gives a direct procedure:
Consistency of \(V\). The parametric bootstrap is valid only if \(V\) consistently estimates \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar{S})\). If \(V\) is systematically too small, the bootstrap null distribution will be too narrow, producing an excess of small p-values. We check this by simulating many datasets under \(H_0\), computing the empirical variance of \(\bar{S}\) across replications, and comparing it to the average of the estimated \(V\). The two should agree.

title: 7  Parametric Bootstrap Test
text:
Compute the observed statistic \(T_\text{obs} = \max_{1 \leq j \leq p} |\bar{S}_j|\).
Draw \(S^{(b)} \sim N(0, V)\) for \(b = 1, \ldots, B\).
Compute \(T^{(b)} = \max_{1 \leq j \leq p} |S^{(b)}_j|\).
The p-value is \(\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \mathbf{1}\!\left[T^{(b)} \geq T_\text{obs}\right]\).

title: 8  Independence Test
text:
8.1 Classical Theory
For jointly Gaussian \((X, Y)\), zero correlation and independence are equivalent, so testing \(H_0: \rho = 0\) is also a test of \(H_0: X \perp Y\). The statistic \(T = \sqrt{n-2}\,\hat\rho / \sqrt{1 - \hat\rho^2}\) follows an exact \(t_{n-2}\) null distribution.
Without the Gaussian assumption, \(\rho = 0\) no longer implies independence — for example, \(X \sim N(0,1)\) and \(Y = X^2\) satisfy \(\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = 0\) but \(X \not\perp Y\). Two approaches handle the non-Gaussian case:
For the weaker null \(H_0: \rho = 0\) without assuming independence, \(\kappa_{22}\) need not equal 1, and the asymptotic variance is \[
v^2 = \frac{1}{n} \left(\omega_x^2 + \omega_y^2 + \kappa_{22} + \frac{5}{2}\right).
\] A robust test plugs in \(\hat\kappa_{22}\).

title: 8  Independence Test
text:
8.2 Estimating \(\kappa_{22}\) via \(W\)
Since lag_terms(X) |> mean() / 2 == ece.cov(X[,1], X[,2]), the sample mean of the \(S_i\) terms satisfies
\[\bar S = \frac{2T_1(X,Y) - T_2(X,Y)}{n},\]
so the parametric bootstrap variance \(W = \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\bar S)\) estimates \(\operatorname{Var}((2T_1-T_2)/n)\). This variance has a closed form containing \(\kappa_{22}\), so we can solve for \(\kappa_{22}\) directly from \(W\).
Under \(H_0\) (\(\sigma_{xy} = 0\)), applying \(\operatorname{Var}(2Z_5 - Z_6) = 4[\Sigma_Z]_{55} - 4[\Sigma_Z]_{56} + [\Sigma_Z]_{66}\) to the entries of \(\Sigma_Z\) gives
\[\operatorname{Var}(2T_1 - T_2) = 2n\!\left[(2\kappa_{22}+5)\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 2\sigma_y^2\omega_x^2 + 2\sigma_x^2\omega_y^2\right].\]
Since \(W = \operatorname{Var}(2T_1 - T_2)/n^2\), solving for \(\kappa_{22}\):
\[\hat\kappa_{22} = \frac{nW}{4\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} - \frac{\hat\omega_x^2}{\hat\sigma_x^2} - \frac{\hat\omega_y^2}{\hat\sigma_y^2} - \frac{5}{2},\]
where \(\hat\omega_x^2 = (T_2(X,X) - T_1(X,X))/n\) and \(\hat\omega_y^2 = (T_2(Y,Y) - T_1(Y,Y))/n\).






Derivation: \(\operatorname{Var}(2T_1 - T_2)\) from \(\Sigma_Z\)





From the \(\Sigma_Z\) table, under \(H_0\) (\(\sigma_{xy} = \omega_{xy} = 0\)):
\[[\Sigma_Z]_{55} = 2n\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2(2\kappa_{22}+1) + 2n\sigma_y^2\omega_x^2 + 2n\sigma_x^2\omega_y^2,\] \[[\Sigma_Z]_{56} = 4n\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2\kappa_{22} + 2n\sigma_y^2\omega_x^2 + 2n\sigma_x^2\omega_y^2,\] \[[\Sigma_Z]_{66} = 2n\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2(2\kappa_{22}+1) + 4n\sigma_y^2\omega_x^2 + 4n\sigma_x^2\omega_y^2.\]
Substituting into \(4[\Sigma_Z]_{55} - 4[\Sigma_Z]_{56} + [\Sigma_Z]_{66}\):

\(\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2\) coefficient: \(4\cdot 2(2\kappa_{22}+1) - 4\cdot 4\kappa_{22} + 2(2\kappa_{22}+1) = 4\kappa_{22} + 10 = 2(2\kappa_{22}+5)\).
\(\sigma_y^2\omega_x^2\) coefficient: \(4\cdot 2 - 4\cdot 2 + 4 = 4\).
\(\sigma_x^2\omega_y^2\) coefficient: \(4\cdot 2 - 4\cdot 2 + 4 = 4\).

Therefore \(\operatorname{Var}(2T_1 - T_2) = 2n[(2\kappa_{22}+5)\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 2\sigma_y^2\omega_x^2 + 2\sigma_x^2\omega_y^2]\).
Since \(W = \operatorname{Var}(2T_1-T_2)/n^2\), we have \(nW/2 = (2\kappa_{22}+5)\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 2\sigma_y^2\omega_x^2 + 2\sigma_x^2\omega_y^2\). Solving:
\[\kappa_{22} = \frac{nW/2 - 2\sigma_y^2\omega_x^2 - 2\sigma_x^2\omega_y^2}{2\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2} - \frac{5}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{1} = \frac{nW}{4\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2} - \frac{\omega_x^2}{\sigma_x^2} - \frac{\omega_y^2}{\sigma_y^2} - \frac{5}{2}. \quad\square\]

title: 9  Simulation Design
text:
9.1 Generating Correlated Errors via Cholesky Decomposition
To simulate errors with a target covariance matrix \(\Sigma\), we use the Cholesky decomposition. Factor \(\Sigma = L^T L\) where \(L\) is upper triangular. Then for any \(n \times p\) matrix \(Z\) with iid entries of mean zero and unit variance,
\[
E = Z L
\]
has \(\text{Cov}(E_t) = L^T \text{Cov}(Z_t) L = L^T L = \Sigma\).
In generate_err, \(L\) = chol(S) and the correlated errors are produced as Z %*% chol(S). The marginal distribution of each entry of \(Z\) — normal, \(t\), log-normal, etc. — determines the marginal distribution of \(\varepsilon_t\), while the covariance structure is always \(\Sigma\) regardless of that choice.

11.4 Variance Difference: General vs. Gaussian
Recall the asymptotic variance under the general and Gaussian assumptions: \[
V = \frac{1}{n}\left[(1-\rho^2)\!\left(\frac{\omega_x^2}{\sigma_x^2} + \frac{\omega_y^2}{\sigma_y^2} - \frac{2\rho\,\omega_{xy}}{\sigma_x\sigma_y}\right) + \frac{\rho^2}{4}(\kappa_{40}+2\kappa_{22}+\kappa_{04}) - \rho(\kappa_{31}+\kappa_{13}) + \frac{5}{2}(1-\rho^2)^2 + \kappa_{22}\right],
\] \[
V_G = \frac{1}{n}(1-\rho^2)\!\left(\frac{\omega_x^2}{\sigma_x^2} + \frac{\omega_y^2}{\sigma_y^2} - \frac{2\rho\,\omega_{xy}}{\sigma_x\sigma_y} + \frac{7}{2}(1-\rho^2)\right).

\] This is zero under the Gaussian assumption and measures the excess variance due to non-Gaussianity.

title: 12  Positive Semidefinite
text:
12.1 Existence of an Unbiased PSD Estimator
The ECE is not guaranteed to be positive semidefinite. In particular, when applied to estimate a variance (\(X = Y\)), the estimator \(\hat{\sigma}_{xx} = X^T A X\) can return negative values, since the matrix \(A\) itself is not positive semidefinite.
If \(A \succeq 0\) and \(\theta_x^T A \theta_y = 0\) for all \(\theta_x, \theta_y \in \Theta_L\), then in particular \(\theta^T A \theta = 0\) for all \(\theta \in \Theta_L\). Since \(A \succeq 0\), all eigenvalues are non-negative. Using the eigendecomposition \(A = Q\Lambda Q^*\) with \(\lambda_j \geq 0\),
\[\theta^T A \theta = \sum_j \lambda_j |\tilde\theta_j|^2 = 0.\]
Since every term is non-negative, each must vanish individually: \(\lambda_j |\tilde\theta_j|^2 = 0\) for all \(j\), so \(\lambda_j \tilde\theta_j = 0\) for all \(j\). Therefore \(A\theta = Q\Lambda\tilde\theta = 0\). This shows that any unbiased PSD estimator must satisfy \(A\theta = 0\) for all \(\theta \in \Theta_L\). If \(\operatorname{span}(\Theta_L) = \mathbb{R}^n\), this forces \(A = 0\), contradicting \(\operatorname{tr}(A) = 1\). Whether \(\Theta_L\) spans \(\mathbb{R}^n\) depends on \(n\) and \(L\) and is not established here.

title: 12  Positive Semidefinite
text:
12.2 PSD Projection via Eigenvalue Clipping
The closest positive semidefinite matrix to \(A\) in Frobenius norm is obtained by replacing negative eigenvalues with zero. Given the eigendecomposition \(A = Q\Lambda Q^*\), define
\[\Lambda_+ = \operatorname{diag}(\max(\lambda_0, 0), \ldots, \max(\lambda_{n-1}, 0))\]
and form
\[A_+ = Q\Lambda_+ Q^*.\]
The resulting estimator \(\hat{\sigma}_{xy}^+ = X^T A_+ Y\) is guaranteed to be non-negative when \(X = Y\), since \(A_+ \succeq 0\). The cost is that \(A_+\) no longer satisfies the unbiasedness constraints.

title: 12  Positive Semidefinite
section: 12.3 Bias Analysis of the PSD Projection
text:
12.3 Bias Analysis of the PSD Projection
The bias of \(\hat{\sigma}_{xy}^+ = X^T A_+ Y\) is
\[
\mathbb{E}[\hat{\sigma}_{xy}^+] = \theta_x^T A_+ \theta_y + \sigma_{xy} \operatorname{tr}(A_+).
\]
By clipping negative eigenvalues, we have \(\operatorname{tr}(A_+) = \sum_{j: \lambda_j \geq 0} \lambda_j < \operatorname{tr}(A) = 1\). The bias is therefore
\[
\text{Bias}(A_+) = \theta_x^T A_+ \theta_y + \sigma_{xy} \left(\operatorname{tr}(A_+) - 1\right).
\]
The second term \(\sigma_{xy}(\operatorname{tr}(A_+) - 1)\) is always negative (when \(\sigma_{xy} > 0\)), introducing systematic downward bias. By clipping, we lose the negative eigenvalue contributions that canceled the positive ones under correct specification. For \(\theta_x, \theta_y \in \Theta_L\), the original cancellation \(\sum_j \lambda_j |\tilde\theta_j|^2 = 0\) becomes a non-cancellation \(\sum_j \lambda_j^+ |\tilde\theta_j|^2 \geq 0\) after clipping, introducing an additional positive spectral bias. The total bias is thus driven by both the trace loss and the broken cancellation, and its magnitude depends on the size and location of the negative eigenvalues in the spectrum.

title: 13  Model Misspecification
text:
13.1 Key Concepts
The signal \(\theta\). A vector \((\theta_0, \ldots, \theta_{n-1})\) where \(\theta_i\) is the true mean of the time series at time \(i\). The ECE is designed for piecewise-constant \(\theta\); misspecification means \(\theta\) has some other shape.
Frequency index \(j\). An integer from \(0\) to \(n-1\) labeling a sinusoidal component. Specifically, \(j\) counts how many complete oscillations the sinusoid \(\cos(2\pi j i / n)\) makes as \(i\) runs from \(0\) to \(n-1\):
The plot below shows what each of these looks like concretely.
The DFT. The Discrete Fourier Transform rewrites \(\theta\) as a sum of sinusoids — one at each frequency \(j\). The complex coefficient \(\tilde\theta_j\) says how much of \(\theta\) oscillates at rate \(j\).
Energy \(|\tilde\theta_j|^2/n\). How much of \(\theta\)’s total variation comes from frequency \(j\). A tall bar at \(j = 5\) means \(\theta\) has a strong 5-cycle-per-window oscillation. By Parseval’s theorem, the energies sum to \(\|\theta\|^2/n\).
Eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\). The ECE matrix \(A\) acts differently on each frequency: it scales sinusoidal components by \(\lambda_j\). Small \(|\lambda_j|\) means the ECE ignores energy at that frequency; large \(|\lambda_j|\) means energy there leaks into the bias.
The bias formula. Because of the eigendecomposition \(A = Q\Lambda Q^*\), the bias simplifies to a frequency-by-frequency weighted sum:
\[\theta^T A \theta = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \lambda_j \cdot \frac{|\tilde\theta_j|^2}{n}\]
This is the central formula for understanding misspecification: the bias is the dot product between the signal’s energy profile and the ECE’s frequency sensitivity. Wherever \(\lambda_j \approx 0\), that frequency contributes nothing to the bias regardless of how much energy \(\theta\) places there.

title: 13  Model Misspecification
text:
13.2 Circulant Matrices and the DFT
Every symmetric circulant \(A = \operatorname{circ}(a)\) is diagonalized by the DFT matrix \(F \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}\),
\[
A = F^* \Lambda F,
\]
where \(F_{jk} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \omega^{jk}\), \(\omega = e^{-2\pi i/n}\), and \(\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_0, \ldots, \lambda_{n-1})\). The eigenvalues are the DFT of the first row:
\[
\lambda_j = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k\, \omega^{jk} = (\mathcal{F} a)_j.
\]
Since \(A\) is real and symmetric, the eigenvalues are real and satisfy \(\lambda_j = \lambda_{n-j}\).
Because \(F\) is unitary (\(F F^* = I\)), the decomposition \(A = F^* \Lambda F\) is exactly the eigendecomposition \(A = Q \Lambda Q^{-1}\) with \(Q = F^*\). The columns of \(F^*\) are the eigenvectors of \(A\): the \(j\)-th eigenvector is \(f_j = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}(1, \omega^{-j}, \omega^{-2j}, \ldots, \omega^{-(n-1)j})^T\), a complex sinusoid at frequency \(j/n\).






DFT and eigendecomposition are the same thing for circulants

Spectral representation of the bias. Using the eigendecomposition \(A = Q\Lambda Q^*\) with \(Q = F^*\),
\[
\theta_x^T A \theta_y = \theta_x^T Q \Lambda Q^* \theta_y = (Q^*\theta_x)^* \Lambda (Q^*\theta_y) = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \lambda_j\, \tilde{\theta}_{x,j}^*\, \tilde{\theta}_{y,j},
\]
where \(\tilde{\theta} = Q^*\theta\) are the coordinates of \(\theta\) in the eigenbasis.
Under correct specification (\(\theta \in \Theta_L\)), the \(j = 0\) term vanishes because \(\lambda_0 = 0\) always — the DC eigenvalue is zero since \(\sum_k a_k = 0\) by the block-sum constraints. For \(j > 0\), neither \(\lambda_j\) nor \(\tilde{\theta}_j\) is zero in general; the sum cancels through structured pairwise cancellation across frequencies, a consequence of the block-sum constraints rather than anything visible in \(\lambda\) or \(\tilde{\theta}\) individually.
The spectral representation is most useful under misspecification. When \(\theta \notin \Theta_L\), the pairwise cancellation breaks down and the bias
\[
\theta_x^T A \theta_y = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \lambda_j\, \tilde{\theta}_{x,j}^*\, \tilde{\theta}_{y,j}
\]
is nonzero. Its magnitude depends on which eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\) are large and how much energy \(\tilde{\theta}_x\), \(\tilde{\theta}_y\) place at the corresponding frequencies.

title: 13  Model Misspecification
text:
13.3 Closed-Form Bias
Since \(A = \sum_{k=1}^L c_k A_k\) with \(c_k = H_{1,k} = \frac{2L+1-3k}{nL(L-1)}\) (see Other Mathematical Results), the bias decomposes as
\[
\theta_x^T A \theta_y = \sum_{k=1}^L c_k\, T_k(\theta_x, \theta_y),
\]
where \(T_k(\theta_x, \theta_y) = \sum_{i=1}^n (\theta_{x,i} - \theta_{x,i+k})(\theta_{y,i} - \theta_{y,i+k})\) is the \(k\)-lagged cross-product of the mean vectors. For \(L = 2\) this reduces to
\[
\theta_x^T A \theta_y = \frac{1}{2n}\bigl(2T_1(\theta_x, \theta_y) - T_2(\theta_x, \theta_y)\bigr).
\]
Spectral form of \(\lambda_j\). Applying the eigendecomposition of \(A_k\) — whose eigenvalues are \(4\sin^2(\pi jk/n)\) — gives a closed form for the eigenvalues of \(A\):
\[
\lambda_j = \sum_{k=1}^L c_k \cdot 4\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi jk}{n}\right) = \frac{4}{nL(L-1)}\sum_{k=1}^L (2L+1-3k)\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi jk}{n}\right).
\]
For \(L = 2\) this simplifies to
\[
\lambda_j = -\frac{4}{n}\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi j}{n}\right)\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi j}{n}\right).
\]
Bias bound. By Cauchy–Schwarz in the eigenbasis, and using \(\|\tilde{\theta}\|_2 = \|\theta\|_2\) (unitarity of \(Q\)),
\[
|\theta_x^T A \theta_y| \leq \max_j |\lambda_j| \cdot \|\theta_x\|_2 \|\theta_y\|_2.
\]
The bias is therefore controlled by \(\max_j |\lambda_j|\), which from the \(L=2\) formula is largest near the Nyquist frequency \(j = n/2\). Misspecification is most harmful when the mean vectors have energy concentrated at high frequencies.

title: 13  Model Misspecification
text:
13.4 Closed-Form Variance
The variance of \(X^T A Y\) is (see the Bilinear Form chapter):
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X^T A Y) = \sigma_y^2\,\theta_x^T A^2 \theta_x + \sigma_x^2\,\theta_y^T A^2 \theta_y + 2\sigma_{xy}\,\theta_x^T A^2 \theta_y + (\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + \sigma_{xy}^2)\operatorname{tr}(A^2).
\]
The noise term \((\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + \sigma_{xy}^2)\operatorname{tr}(A^2) = O(1/n)\) regardless of the mean. The signal-dependent terms involve \(\theta_x^T A^2 \theta_y\), which mirrors the bias with \(A\) replaced by \(A^2\).
Spectral form. Since \(A^2 = Q\Lambda^2 Q^*\),
\[
\theta_x^T A^2 \theta_y = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \lambda_j^2\, \tilde{\theta}_{x,j}^*\, \tilde{\theta}_{y,j},
\]
where \(\tilde{\theta} = Q^*\theta\). This is the spectral bias formula with \(\lambda_j\) replaced by \(\lambda_j^2\).
Spectral form of \(\lambda_j^2\). For \(L = 2\), squaring \(\lambda_j = -\frac{4}{n}\cos(2\pi j/n)\sin^2(\pi j/n)\):
\[
\lambda_j^2 = \frac{16}{n^2}\cos^2\!\left(\frac{2\pi j}{n}\right)\sin^4\!\left(\frac{\pi j}{n}\right).
\]
Variance bound. By Cauchy–Schwarz in the eigenbasis:
\[
|\theta_x^T A^2 \theta_y| \leq \max_j \lambda_j^2 \cdot \|\theta_x\|_2 \|\theta_y\|_2 = \left(\max_j |\lambda_j|\right)^2 \|\theta_x\|_2 \|\theta_y\|_2.
\]
The signal-dependent variance is controlled by the same Nyquist-dominated \(\max_j|\lambda_j|\) as the bias.

title: 13  Model Misspecification
text:
13.5 Case Study: Sinusoidal Mean
Suppose \(\theta_x = \theta_y = \theta\) with \(\theta_i = A\sin(2\pi fi/n)\) for integer frequency \(1 \leq f < n/2\) and amplitude \(A > 0\). This is misspecified since a sinusoid is not piecewise constant.

13.5.1 Bias
Computing \(T_k(\theta, \theta)\). Applying the sum-to-product identity \(\sin\alpha - \sin\beta = 2\cos\!\left(\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}\right)\sin\!\left(\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}\right)\),
\[
\theta_i - \theta_{i+k} = -2A\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi fk}{n}\right)\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi fi}{n} + \frac{\pi fk}{n}\right).
\]
Squaring and summing over \(i\), and using \(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\cos^2(\alpha + 2\pi fi/n) = n/2\) for \(f \neq 0\),
\[
T_k(\theta, \theta) = 2nA^2\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi fk}{n}\right).
\]
Bias for \(L = 2\). Substituting into \(\frac{1}{2n}(2T_1 - T_2)\),
\[
\theta^T A \theta = 2A^2\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi f}{n}\right) - A^2\sin^2\!\left(\frac{2\pi f}{n}\right).
\]
Using \(\sin^2(2\phi) = 4\sin^2(\phi)\cos^2(\phi)\) and the double-angle identity \(1 - 2\cos^2\phi = -\cos(2\phi)\),
\[
\theta^T A \theta = -2A^2\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi f}{n}\right)\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi f}{n}\right).
\]
Interpretation. The bias depends on frequency and amplitude but not on phase. It is zero at \(f = 0\) (constant — well specified) and at \(f = n/4\) (where \(\cos(2\pi f/n) = 0\)), negative for \(f < n/4\), and positive for \(f > n/4\). It grows as \(A^2\) and is largest near the Nyquist frequency \(f = n/2\), consistent with the general bound \(|\text{bias}| \leq \max_j|\lambda_j| \cdot \|\theta\|_2^2\).

devtools::load_all("..")
library(testthat)

n <- 40; L <- 2
a     <- ece_reg_row(n, L)
A_mat <- circ(a) / n
freqs <- 1:(n/2 - 1)

bias_numerical <- sapply(freqs, function(f) {
  theta <- sin(2 * pi * f * (0:(n - 1)) / n)
  as.numeric(t(theta) %*% A_mat %*% theta)
})

bias_formula <- -2 * sin(pi * freqs / n)^2 * cos(2 * pi * freqs / n)

test_that("sinusoidal bias matches closed form", {
  expect_equal(bias_numerical, bias_formula, tolerance = 1e-10)
})

Test passed 🥇

plot(freqs, bias_formula,
  type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "steelblue",
  xlab = "Frequency f", ylab = "Bias",
  main = "Bias for sinusoidal mean (A = 1, L = 2)"
)
abline(h = 0, col = "grey60", lty = 2)








Application to scenario 14. Scenario 14 sets \(\theta_i = \sin(2\pi i / 365)\) — a yearly cycle sampled at daily resolution. With \(n = 100\) observations, the signal has effective DFT bin \(j \approx n/365 \approx 0.27\), well below \(j = 1\). Since \(\lambda_j \approx 0\) near \(j = 0\), the formula predicts negligible bias: \(|\text{bias}| \approx 2\sin^2(\pi/365) \approx 1.5 \times 10^{-4}\) per unit amplitude squared. Numerically the bias is of order \(10^{-5}\), confirming that the ECE is effectively unbiased in this scenario despite the misspecification — the yearly cycle is too slow relative to the observation window to contaminate the estimate.
With \(n = 1000\) observations, the window covers approximately 2.7 full periods and the effective bin shifts to \(j \approx 2.74\). The bias is now \(\approx -1.6 \times 10^{-4}\) — negative since \(j < n/4 = 250\), and consistent with the formula prediction of \(-1.5 \times 10^{-4}\). Despite the larger signal (\(\|\theta\|^2 \approx 499\)), the bias remains negligible: the yearly cycle is still low-frequency relative to \(n\).


13.5.2 Variance
With \(\theta_x = \theta_y = \theta\), the closed-form variance simplifies to
\[\operatorname{Var}(X^T A Y) = (\sigma_x^2 + \sigma_y^2 + 2\sigma_{xy})\,\theta^T A^2 \theta + (\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + \sigma_{xy}^2)\operatorname{tr}(A^2).\]
Computing \(\theta^T A^2 \theta\). Since \(\theta_i = A\sin(2\pi fi/n)\) lies in the eigenspace of \(A\) at frequency \(f\) and \(\lambda_f = \lambda_{n-f}\), we have \(A\theta = \lambda_f\,\theta\). Therefore \(\theta^T A^2 \theta = \lambda_f^2\|\theta\|^2 = \frac{nA^2}{2}\lambda_f^2\).
For \(L = 2\). Substituting the \(L=2\) eigenvalue:
\[\operatorname{Var}(X^T A Y) = \frac{8A^2}{n}(\sigma_x^2 + \sigma_y^2 + 2\sigma_{xy})\cos^2\!\left(\frac{2\pi f}{n}\right)\sin^4\!\left(\frac{\pi f}{n}\right) + (\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + \sigma_{xy}^2)\operatorname{tr}(A^2).\]
Both terms are \(O(1/n)\). The signal-dependent term vanishes at the same frequencies as the bias (\(f = 0\) and \(f = n/4\)).

library(testthat)

n <- 40; L <- 2
a      <- ece_reg_row(n, L)
A_mat  <- circ(a) / n
lambda <- Re(fft(a) / n)
freqs  <- 1:(n/2 - 1)

test_that("A * theta = lambda_f * theta for sinusoidal theta", {
  for (f in freqs) {
    theta <- sin(2 * pi * f * (0:(n - 1)) / n)
    expect_equal(as.numeric(A_mat %*% theta), lambda[f + 1] * theta,
                 tolerance = 1e-10)
  }
})

  theta <- sin(2 * pi * f * (0:(n - 1)) / n)
  as.numeric(t(theta) %*% A_mat %*% A_mat %*% theta)

Test passed 🎊

title: 13  Model Misspecification
text:
13.6 Case Study: Random Walk Mean
Suppose \(\theta_x = \theta_y = \theta\) where \(\theta_i = \sum_{j=1}^i \xi_j\) is a random walk with i.i.d. increments \(\xi_j \sim (0, \sigma^2)\). This corresponds to scenario 13.
Expected bias is \(O(1/n)\). Since \(\theta_i - \theta_{i+k} = \xi_{i+1} + \cdots + \xi_{i+k}\) is a sum of \(k\) independent increments,
\[
E\bigl[(\theta_i - \theta_{i+k})^2\bigr] = k\sigma^2,
\]






Why \(E[(\theta_i - \theta_{i+k})^2] = k\sigma^2\)





The lag-\(k\) difference telescopes into a sum of exactly \(k\) consecutive increments:
\[\theta_i - \theta_{i+k} = -(\xi_{i+1} + \cdots + \xi_{i+k})\]
Since the \(\xi_t\) are i.i.d. with mean 0 and variance \(\sigma^2\), squaring and taking expectations gives:
\[E[(\theta_i - \theta_{i+k})^2] = \sum_{s=i+1}^{i+k} \sum_{t=i+1}^{i+k} E[\xi_s \xi_t] = \sum_{s=i+1}^{i+k} \sigma^2 = k\sigma^2\]
where the cross terms \(E[\xi_s \xi_t] = 0\) for \(s \neq t\) by independence.
Summing over \(i = 1, \ldots, n-k\) (the valid pairs) then gives \(E[T_k] = (n-k)k\sigma^2\). For \(k \ll n\) this is approximately \(nk\sigma^2\), linear in \(k\).



so \(E[T_k(\theta,\theta)] = (n-k)k\sigma^2\), which is approximately linear in \(k\) for \(k \ll n\). Since the ECE is constructed to cancel exactly a linear trend in \(k \mapsto T_k\),
\[
E[\theta^T A \theta] = \frac{1}{2n}\bigl(2(n-1)\sigma^2 - 2(n-2)\sigma^2\bigr) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n} \to 0.
\]
The expected bias vanishes asymptotically — the ECE is nearly unbiased in expectation for random walk means, even though random walks are not piecewise constant.
Spectral interpretation. The power spectral density of a random walk concentrates at low frequencies: \(E[|\tilde{\theta}_j|^2] \propto 1/\sin^2(\pi j/n)\). Combined with \(\lambda_j \propto -\cos(2\pi j/n)\sin^2(\pi j/n)\), the expected bias is proportional to \(\sum_j \cos(2\pi j/n) = 0\), confirming the result.
Individual realizations. While \(E[\theta^T A \theta] \approx 0\), each realization of the random walk produces a nonzero bias. The distribution of realized biases has mean \(\approx \sigma^2/n\) and standard deviation that grows with \(\sigma^2\).

n <- 100; L <- 2
a     <- ece_reg_row(n, L)
A_mat <- circ(a) / n

set.seed(42)
B      <- 5000
biases <- replicate(B, {
  theta <- cumsum(rnorm(n))
  as.numeric(t(theta) %*% A_mat %*% theta)
})

test_that("expected bias is close to sigma^2/n = 1/100", {
  expect_equal(mean(biases), 1 / n, tolerance = 0.05)
})

  breaks = 60, col = "steelblue", border = "white",

title: 13  Model Misspecification
text:
13.7 Spectral Fingerprints of Common Misspecifications
Each misspecification has a characteristic frequency signature. The left panel shows \(\theta_i\); the right panel shows its power spectrum \(|\tilde\theta_j|^2/n\) (bars, left axis) together with the ECE eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\) (red line, right axis). The bias \(\theta^T A \theta = \sum_j \lambda_j |\tilde\theta_j|^2/n\) is the inner product between the two curves — large only when signal energy and \(|\lambda_j|\) overlap at the same frequencies.

devtools::load_all("..")

n <- 100; L <- 2
set.seed(42)

a          <- ece_reg_row(n, L)
A_mat      <- circ(a) / n
lambda_all <- Re(fft(a) / n)
j_pos      <- 1:(n / 2)          # unique positive-frequency indices (1-based)
lambda_pos <- lambda_all[j_pos + 1]

make_scenario <- function(name, theta) {
  bias  <- as.numeric(t(theta) %*% A_mat %*% theta)
  power <- Mod(fft(theta))^2 / n  # Parseval-normalised
  list(name = name, theta = theta, bias = bias, power = power[j_pos + 1])
}

scenarios <- list(
  make_scenario("Linear",         (0:(n - 1) - (n - 1) / 2) / n),
  make_scenario("Step (-1 to 1)", ifelse(0:(n - 1) < n / 2, -1, 1)),
  make_scenario("Sinusoid",       sin(2 * pi * 10 * (0:(n - 1)) / n)),
  make_scenario("Random Walk",    cumsum(rnorm(n)))
)

par(mfrow = c(4, 2), mar = c(3.5, 3.5, 2.5, 4.5))

for (sc in scenarios) {
  ## Left: time domain
  plot(0:(n - 1), sc$theta, type = "l", lwd = 1.5, col = "steelblue",
       xlab = "i", ylab = expression(theta[i]),
       main = bquote(.(sc$name) ~ "  [bias =" ~ .(round(sc$bias, 5)) ~ "]"))

  ## Right: power spectrum (primary axis) + lambda_j (secondary axis)
  ylim_power <- c(0, max(sc$power) * 1.15)
  ylim_lam   <- range(lambda_pos) * c(1.2, 1.2)

  plot(j_pos, sc$power, type = "h", lwd = 2,
       col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.6),
       xlab = "Frequency j", ylab = expression("|" ~ tilde(theta)[j] ~ "|"^2 / n),
       main = "Spectrum",
       ylim = ylim_power)
  abline(h = 0, col = "grey70", lty = 2)

  par(new = TRUE)
  plot(j_pos, lambda_pos, type = "l", col = "firebrick", lwd = 2,
       axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       ylim = ylim_lam)
  axis(4, col = "firebrick", col.axis = "firebrick", las = 1)
  mtext(expression(lambda[j]), side = 4, line = 3, col = "firebrick")
  abline(h = 0, col = "firebrick", lty = 3, lwd = 0.8)
}

title: 13  Model Misspecification
text:
13.8 Linear Signals at Different Slopes
A natural conjecture is that steeper linear signals shift spectral energy to higher frequencies, producing more bias. The figures below test this: \(\theta_i = m \cdot (i/n - 0.5)\) for slopes \(m = 1, 2, 5, 10\).









The spectral shape is identical across all slopes — energy concentrates at low \(j\) in every case. What changes is only the scale: the bars grow as \(m^2\). Since \(\lambda_j \approx 0\) at those low frequencies, the bias remains small even for steep slopes. A linear signal is inherently low-frequency, and the ECE is insensitive to low-frequency structure by construction.

title: 13  Model Misspecification
text:
13.9 Eigenvalue Visualization
Each eigenvalue \(\lambda_j = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k \omega^{jk}\) is a sum of \(n\) complex numbers. The plot below shows the individual terms \(a_k \omega^{jk}\) for \(k = 0, \ldots, n-1\) as arrows in the complex plane, for each \(j\). The red star marks the sum \(\lambda_j\), which is always real.

devtools::load_all("..")

n <- 10
L <- 2
a <- ece_first_row(n, L)
a[abs(a) < 1e-10] <- 0
omega <- exp(-2i * pi / n)

par(mfrow = c(2, 5), mar = c(3, 3, 2, 1))

for (j in 0:(n - 1)) {
  k     <- 0:(n - 1)
  terms <- a * omega^(j * k)
  lim   <- max(abs(c(Re(terms), Im(terms))), 0.5) * 1.3

  plot(Re(terms), Im(terms),
    xlim = c(-lim, lim), ylim = c(-lim, lim),
    xlab = "Re", ylab = "Im", asp = 1,
    main = bquote(j == .(j) ~ "," ~ lambda[.(j)] == .(round(Re(sum(terms)), 3))),
    pch = 16, col = "steelblue"
  )
  abline(h = 0, v = 0, col = "grey80", lty = 2)
  arrows(0, 0, Re(terms), Im(terms), length = 0.07, col = "steelblue", lwd = 1.2)
  points(Re(sum(terms)), Im(sum(terms)), pch = 8, col = "red", cex = 1.5, lwd = 2)
}

section: A.2 SVD for Identifying the Null Space
text:
A.2 SVD for Identifying the Null Space
Given the constraint matrix \(G \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\), the singular value decomposition is: \[G = U \Sigma V^T\] where \(U \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times m}\) and \(V \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\) are orthogonal matrices, and \(\Sigma\) is a diagonal matrix with singular values \(\sigma_1 \geq \sigma_2 \geq \cdots \geq \sigma_{\min(m,n)} \geq 0\).

A.2.1 Connection to the Null Space
The null space of \(G\) is: \[\text{null}(G) = \{a \in \mathbb{R}^n : Ga = 0\}\]
If \(G\) has rank \(r < n\), the right singular vectors corresponding to zero singular values span the null space: \[\text{null}(G) = \text{span}\{v_{r+1}, v_{r+2}, \ldots, v_n\}\] where \(v_i\) are the columns of \(V\).


A.2.2 Steps to Identify the Null Space

Compute the SVD: \(G = U \Sigma V^T\)
Identify the rank \(r\) as the number of non-zero singular values
Extract the right singular vectors \(v_{r+1}, \ldots, v_n\) corresponding to the zero singular values
The null space basis is \(\text{null}(G) = \text{span}\{v_{r+1}, \ldots, v_n\}\)

title: Appendix A — Computational Solution
text:
A.3 Pseudoinverse and Min-Norm Solution
The Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse \(G^+\) is defined via SVD as: \[G^+ = V \Sigma^+ U^T\] where \(\Sigma^+\) is obtained by taking reciprocals of the non-zero singular values and transposing.
\(G^+\) simultaneously solves two optimality problems. When \(b \notin \text{col}(G)\) the system \(Ga = b\) is inconsistent, and \(G^+b\) is the least-squares solution minimizing \(\|Ga - b\|_2^2\). When the system is consistent but underdetermined, \(G^+b\) is the minimum-norm solution among all exact solutions.
For a system \(Ga = b\), the general solution is: \[a = G^+ b + \sum_{i=r+1}^{n} c_i v_i\] where the second term spans \(\text{null}(G)\). The norm of the general solution is: \[\|a\|^2 = \|G^+ b\|^2 + \sum_{i=r+1}^{n} c_i^2\] since \(G^+ b\) lies in the row space of \(G\), which is orthogonal to \(\text{null}(G)\). This is minimized by setting all \(c_i = 0\), giving the minimum-norm solution: \[a^* = G^+ b\]

title: Appendix B — Mean Removal
text:
B.1 Segmentation
Assume each time series has a piecewise-constant mean: \[X_t = \mu_t + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \mu_t \text{ piecewise constant.}\] Segmentation estimates \(\mu_t\) by the within-segment sample mean and subtracts it: \[\hat{\varepsilon}_t = X_t - \hat{\mu}_t.\] The residuals \(\hat{\varepsilon}_t\) are approximately stationary, so Pearson correlation applied to \((\hat{\varepsilon}_t^{(1)}, \hat{\varepsilon}_t^{(2)})\) estimates contemporaneous correlation between the two series.

title: Appendix B — Mean Removal
text:
B.2 Degrees of Freedom Correction
To do inference on Pearson correlation, we first estimate the correlation \(\hat{r}\). Then, we find that \[t_{\text{naive}} = \frac{r \sqrt{n-2}}{\sqrt{1-r^2}} \sim t_{n-2}.\] That is, the standard Pearson correlation has \(df = n-2\), because we use two degrees of freedom to estimate the mean and variance.
However, with segmentation, we must estimate multiple means. If there are \(K\) change points, then we must estimate \(K + 1\) sample means. In all, we must estimate \(K + 2\) parameters, so the correct statistic is \[t_{\text{correct}} = \frac{r\sqrt{n-K-2}}{\sqrt{1-r^2}} \sim t_{n-K-2}.\] Since both statistics share the same \(r\), they are related by \[t_{\text{naive}} = \lambda \cdot t_{\text{correct}}, \qquad \lambda = \sqrt{\frac{n-2}{n-K-2}} > 1.\]
The naive test rejects when \[|t_{\text{naive}}| > t_{n-2,\,\alpha/2}.\] Substituting \(t_{\text{naive}} = \lambda \cdot t_{\text{correct}}\), this is equivalent to \[|t_{\text{correct}}| > \frac{t_{n-2,\,\alpha/2}}{\lambda}.\] So the actual type I error of the naive test is \[P\!\left(|t_{\text{correct}}| > \frac{t_{n-2,\,\alpha/2}}{\lambda}\right), \qquad t_{\text{correct}} \sim t_{n-K-2}.\] Since \(\lambda > 1\), the threshold \(t_{n-2,\,\alpha/2}/\lambda < t_{n-K-2,\,\alpha/2}\), so the naive test rejects more often than it should.
Theoretical type I error. Given \(n\), \(K\), and \(\alpha\), the exact inflation is computable in closed form. Let \(c = t_{n-2,\,\alpha/2}\) be the naive critical value. The actual type I error is \[P\!\left(|T| > \frac{c}{\lambda}\right), \qquad T \sim t_{n-K-2}.\] In R: 2 * pt(-qt(1 - alpha/2, df = n-2) / lambda, df = n - K - 2).

title: Appendix C — Mathematical Background
text:
C.1 Expectation and Variance of Linear Transformations
For a random vector \(X\) and a fixed matrix \(A\):
\[
\mathbb{E}[AX] = A\,\mathbb{E}[X], \qquad \operatorname{Var}(AX) = A\operatorname{Var}(X)A^T.
\]
For a scalar linear form \(a^T X\), these specialize to
\[
\mathbb{E}[a^T X] = a^T \mathbb{E}[X], \qquad \operatorname{Var}(a^T X) = a^T \operatorname{Var}(X)\, a.
\]

title: Appendix C — Mathematical Background
section: C.2 Trace Trick for Quadratic Forms
text:
C.2 Trace Trick for Quadratic Forms
For any scalar \(z\), \(z = \operatorname{tr}(z)\). So for vectors \(u, v\) and a fixed matrix \(A\),
\[
u^T A v = \operatorname{tr}(u^T A v).
\]
Applying the cyclic property of trace, \(\operatorname{tr}(u^T A v) = \operatorname{tr}(A v u^T)\). Taking expectations and using linearity,
\[
\mathbb{E}[u^T A v] = \operatorname{tr}\!\left(A\,\mathbb{E}[v u^T]\right).
\]
In particular, if \(u = \varepsilon_x\) and \(v = \varepsilon_y\) with cross-covariance \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_y \varepsilon_x^T] = \Sigma_{xy}\), then
\[
\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y] = \operatorname{tr}(A \Sigma_{xy}).
\]

title: Appendix C — Mathematical Background
text:
C.3 Properties of Circulant Matrices
Let \(C_1 = \operatorname{circ}(0, 1, 0, \ldots, 0)\) be the elementary shift-by-one matrix, so \(C_1^k = C_k\). The following facts hold:

Power. \(C_k = C_1^k\), so applying a shift of \(k\) is the same as applying a shift of 1 exactly \(k\) times. As a consequence, every circulant matrix is a polynomial in \(C_1\): \(\operatorname{circ}(a_0, \ldots, a_{n-1}) = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k C_1^k\).
Transpose. \(C_k^T = C_{n-k} = C_k^{-1}\), since \(C_k\) is a permutation matrix.
Circulant form. \(C_k = \operatorname{circ}(e_k)\), where \(e_k\) is the standard basis vector with a 1 in position \(k\) and 0s elsewhere. That is, \(C_k\) is the circulant matrix whose first row has a single 1 on the \(k\)-th band.

title: Appendix C — Mathematical Background
section: C.4 Spectral Properties of Circulant Matrices
text:
C.4 Spectral Properties of Circulant Matrices
Every circulant matrix \(A = \operatorname{circ}(a_0, \ldots, a_{n-1})\) is diagonalized by the DFT matrix \(F\),
\[
A = F^* \Lambda F, \qquad F_{jk} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\,\omega^{jk}, \quad \omega = e^{-2\pi i/n},
\]
where indices \(j, k\) run from \(0\) to \(n-1\). Since \(F\) is unitary (\(FF^* = I\)), this is the eigendecomposition \(A = Q\Lambda Q^{-1}\) with \(Q = F^*\).
Eigenvalues. The \(j\)-th eigenvalue is the DFT of the first row evaluated at frequency \(j\):
\[
\lambda_j = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k\,\omega^{jk}.
\]
Eigenvectors. The columns of \(Q = F^*\) are the eigenvectors. The \(j\)-th eigenvector is
\[
q_j = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\bigl(1,\, \omega^{-j},\, \omega^{-2j},\, \ldots,\, \omega^{-(n-1)j}\bigr)^T,
\]
a complex sinusoid at frequency \(j/n\).
Real symmetric case. When \(A\) is real and symmetric (i.e. \(a_k = a_{n-k}\)), the eigenvalues are real and come in symmetric pairs: \(\lambda_j = \lambda_{n-j}\).

title: Appendix C — Mathematical Background
section: C.5 Variance of a Product of Correlated Standard Normals
text:
C.5 Variance of a Product of Correlated Standard Normals
Let \((z_x, z_y)\) be a standard bivariate Gaussian with zero mean, unit variances, and correlation \(\rho\). Then
\[
\operatorname{Var}(z_x z_y) = 1 + \rho^2.
\]
Proof. Decompose \(z_y = \rho z_x + \sqrt{1 - \rho^2}\, w\) where \(w \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\) is independent of \(z_x\). Then
\[
z_x z_y = \rho z_x^2 + \sqrt{1 - \rho^2}\, z_x w.
\]
Since \(z_x \perp w\), the two terms are independent, so their variances add:
\[
\operatorname{Var}(z_x z_y) = \rho^2 \operatorname{Var}(z_x^2) + (1 - \rho^2)\operatorname{Var}(z_x w).
\]
For \(z_x \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\): \(\operatorname{Var}(z_x^2) = \mathbb{E}[z_x^4] - (\mathbb{E}[z_x^2])^2 = 3 - 1 = 2\). For independent standard normals: \(\operatorname{Var}(z_x w) = \mathbb{E}[z_x^2]\mathbb{E}[w^2] = 1\). Therefore,
\[
\operatorname{Var}(z_x z_y) = 2\rho^2 + (1 - \rho^2) = 1 + \rho^2. \qquad \square
\]

title: Appendix D — Other Mathematical Results
text:
D.1 Properties of \(A^2\)
Let \(A\) be a symmetric circulant with first row \((a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_{n-1})\) and eigenvalues \(\lambda_0, \ldots, \lambda_{n-1}\).
Structure. Since the product of two circulants is circulant and \((A^2)^T = (A^T)^2 = A^2\), \(A^2\) is also a symmetric circulant. Its first row has \(j\)-th entry given by the autocorrelation
\[
(A^2)_j = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k\, a_{j - k \bmod n}.
\]
Positive semidefiniteness. For any vector \(x\), \(x^T A^2 x = \|Ax\|^2 \geq 0\), so \(A^2 \succeq 0\).
Eigenvalues. The eigenvalues of \(A^2\) are \(\lambda_k^2\), so
\[
\operatorname{tr}(A^2) = \sum_k \lambda_k^2 = \|A\|_F^2.
\]
Explicit trace formula. Since every row of a circulant is a cyclic permutation of the first row, each row has the same squared norm, giving
\[
\operatorname{tr}(A^2) = \|A\|_F^2 = n \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k^2 = n\!\left(a_0^2 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor} a_k^2\right),
\]
where the last equality uses the symmetry \(a_k = a_{n-k}\).

title: Appendix D — Other Mathematical Results
text:
D.2 Lower Bound on \(\operatorname{tr}(A^2)\)
Since \(\operatorname{tr}(A) = \sum_i \lambda_i = 1\) and \(\operatorname{tr}(A^2) = \sum_i \lambda_i^2\), Jensen’s inequality gives
\[
\operatorname{tr}(A^2) = \sum_i \lambda_i^2 \geq \frac{\left(\sum_i \lambda_i\right)^2}{n} = \frac{1}{n},
\]
with equality when all eigenvalues are equal. Thus the noise contribution \((\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + \sigma_{xy}^2)\operatorname{tr}(A^2) = O(1/n)\), which shows the estimator is consistent.

title: Appendix D — Other Mathematical Results
text:
D.3 Closed Form of \((K^TK)^{-1}K^T\)
The design matrix is \(K \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times 2}\) with \(K_{k,1} = 1\) and \(K_{k,2} = k\) for \(k = 1, \ldots, L\). We use the Gaussian sum identities
\[\sum_{k=1}^L 1 = L, \qquad \sum_{k=1}^L k = \frac{L(L+1)}{2}, \qquad \sum_{k=1}^L k^2 = \frac{L(L+1)(2L+1)}{6}.\]
Step 1: Compute \(K^TK\).
\[K^TK = \begin{bmatrix} L & \dfrac{L(L+1)}{2} \\[6pt] \dfrac{L(L+1)}{2} & \dfrac{L(L+1)(2L+1)}{6} \end{bmatrix}.\]
Step 2: Compute \(\det(K^TK)\).
\[\det(K^TK) = \frac{L^2(L+1)(2L+1)}{6} - \frac{L^2(L+1)^2}{4} = L^2(L+1)\cdot\frac{2(2L+1) - 3(L+1)}{12} = \frac{L^2(L^2-1)}{12}.\]
Step 3: Invert \(K^TK\).
Applying the \(2\times 2\) inverse formula and simplifying,
\[
(K^TK)^{-1} = \frac{12}{L^2(L^2-1)}\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{L(L+1)(2L+1)}{6} & -\dfrac{L(L+1)}{2} \\[6pt] -\dfrac{L(L+1)}{2} & L \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2(2L+1)}{L(L-1)} & \dfrac{-6}{L(L-1)} \\[6pt] \dfrac{-6}{L(L-1)} & \dfrac{12}{L(L-1)(L+1)} \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Step 4: Multiply by \(K^T\).
The \(j\)-th column of \((K^TK)^{-1}K^T\) is \((K^TK)^{-1}(1,j)^T\). Computing each row,
\[
\bigl((K^TK)^{-1}K^T\bigr)_{1,j} = \frac{2(2L+1)}{L(L-1)} - \frac{6j}{L(L-1)} = \frac{2(2L+1-3j)}{L(L-1)},
\] \[
\bigl((K^TK)^{-1}K^T\bigr)_{2,j} = \frac{-6}{L(L-1)} + \frac{12j}{L(L-1)(L+1)} = \frac{6(2j - L - 1)}{L(L-1)(L+1)}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
(K^TK)^{-1}K^T = \frac{1}{L(L-1)}\begin{bmatrix} 2(2L+1-3j) \\[4pt] \dfrac{6(2j-L-1)}{L+1} \end{bmatrix}_{j=1}^{L}.
\]
Since \(H = \frac{1}{2n}(K^TK)^{-1}K^T\), the first row is
\[H_{1,j} = \frac{2L+1-3j}{nL(L-1)},\]
which is linear in \(j\).

title: 8  Independence Test
text:
Permutation test. Permuting \(Y\) breaks any dependence on \(X\) while preserving marginals, giving an exact test of \(H_0: X \perp Y\) under any distribution.
Asymptotic test of independence. Under \(H_0: X \perp Y\), the errors are independent, so \(\kappa_{22} = 1\) and \(\sqrt{n}\,\hat\rho \xrightarrow{d} N(0, 1)\).

title: 8  Independence Test
text:
8.2 Estimating \(\kappa_{22}\) via \(V\)
Let \(s_i^{(k)} = (X_i - X_{i+k})(Y_i - Y_{i+k})\) and \(S_i = s_i^{(1)} + s_{i+1}^{(1)} - s_i^{(2)}\) as in the Multiplier Bootstrap chapter, so that \[
\bar{S} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n S_i = \frac{2T_1(X,Y) - T_2(X,Y)}{n}
\] is twice the ECE covariance estimator. Define the lag-2 variance estimate \[
V := \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\bar{S}) = \frac{1}{n^2}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n S_i^2 + \sum_{i=1}^n (S_i S_{i+1} + S_{i+1} S_i) + \sum_{i=1}^n (S_i S_{i+2} + S_{i+2} S_i)\right).
\]
Since \(\bar S = (2T_1 - T_2)/n\), we have \(V \approx \operatorname{Var}(2T_1 - T_2)/n^2\). Under \(H_0\) (\(\sigma_{xy} = 0\)), the variance on the right has a closed form in \(\kappa_{22}\), so we can solve for \(\kappa_{22}\) from \(V\).






Derivation: \(\operatorname{Var}(2T_1 - T_2)\) from \(\Sigma_Z\)





Under \(H_0\) (\(\sigma_{xy} = 0\)), \[
\operatorname{Var}(2T_1 - T_2) = 4[\Sigma_Z]_{55} - 4[\Sigma_Z]_{56} + [\Sigma_Z]_{66}.
\] Plugging in the \(\Sigma_Z\) entries from the Z-Test chapter, \[[\Sigma_Z]_{55} = 2n\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2(2\kappa_{22}+1) + 2n\sigma_y^2\omega_x^2 + 2n\sigma_x^2\omega_y^2,\] \[[\Sigma_Z]_{56} = 4n\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2\kappa_{22} + 2n\sigma_y^2\omega_x^2 + 2n\sigma_x^2\omega_y^2,\] \[[\Sigma_Z]_{66} = 2n\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2(2\kappa_{22}+1) + 4n\sigma_y^2\omega_x^2 + 4n\sigma_x^2\omega_y^2,\] and simplifying, \[\operatorname{Var}(2T_1 - T_2) = 2n\bigl[(2\kappa_{22}+5)\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 2\sigma_y^2\omega_x^2 + 2\sigma_x^2\omega_y^2\bigr]. \qquad\square\]



Since \(nV \approx \operatorname{Var}(2T_1-T_2)/n\), substituting and solving gives \[\hat\kappa_{22} = \frac{nV}{4\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} - \frac{\hat\omega_x^2}{\hat\sigma_x^2} - \frac{\hat\omega_y^2}{\hat\sigma_y^2} - \frac{5}{2}.\]
